sections.title: 5.1 Experiment I: With or without Trajectory supervision?
sections.text:
In recent NAR research, there has been a trend of supervising models with additional ground-truth trajectories, which has led to noticeable improvements in reasoning ability [23, 25]. A plausible explanation is that these additional supervisions implicitly break down the original complex problem into smaller, more manageable sub-problems [17, 26]. When only input-output pairs are provided, the model must independently discover how to mimic the reasoning process, which is intuitively more challenging than training with trajectory supervision. Our first experiment investigates the two distinctive training modes: a) with trajectory supervision, and b) without trajectory supervision. Specifically, DFA-GNN+, DFA-GNN, and DFA-GNN− are respectively trained on POJ-104/0/50. As discussed earlier in Section 5, datasets with much larger sample sizes, such as POJ-104/500/600, POJ-104/600/700, and others, are used for testing. The results are presented in Table 1. From the table we can see, if trained without trajectory supervision, a GNN’s generalization performance aligns with its its algorithmic alignment to the DFA algorithm. DFA-GNN+ generalizes nearly perfectly on samples up to twenty times larger (POJ-104/900/1000). Its strong mean step F1 scores suggest that the model accurately predicts nearly every step to reach the final result, demonstrating that DFA-GNN+ has learned to reason like the DFA algorithm from inputoutput pairs alone. In comparison, DFA-GNN performs less efectively in this without-trajectory training mode, while DFA-GNN− fails completely on larger test samples. Table 1. To investigate the reason behind this intriguing phenomenon, we choose a representative test dataset, POJ-104/500/600, and plot the average of the F1 score for each prediction step. As shown in Fig.3, a clear diference emerges between the two training modes: • when DFA-GNN and DFA-GNN− are trained without trajectory supervision, the correctness is low at the beginning and improved in a few steps before becoming stable or dropped; • with trajectory supervision, DFA-GNN−’s performance is nearly perfect initially but gradually decreases over the steps. We argue that the performance patern under the trajectory-supervised training mode is more explainable since it is in line with the real reasoning process of an algorithm — a little mistake may happen somewhere at the beginning, but since the reasoning procedure continues based on the flawed intermediate result, the mistake will be propagated and amplified, eventually leading to degraded final predictions. All subsequent experiments are conducted under the trajectory-supervised training mode.

sections.title: 5.2 Experiment II: Can GNNs learn from truncated trajectories?
sections.text:
Reflecting on how we learned DFA algorithms in class: the teacher would show students a few steps of calculating the next data-flow states based on the current ones, typically using simplified code examples with relatively few statements as demonstrations. After seeing a few examples, most students could handle the entire process, even when dealing with real-world samples containing hundreds of statements that require many steps to reach the final result. The clear advantages of human learners are their high sample eficiency and strong generalization ability across diferent sample sizes and execution trace lengths. Inspired by this, the experiment explores how DFA-GNN+, DFA-GNN, and DFA-GNN− perform when trained on smaller-scale samples with truncated, short trajectories, mimicking how human students learn. Specifically, we extract short continuous portions of trajectories from each sample in POJ-104/0/50, creating three new training datasets: POJ-104/0/50 with 10 steps left, with 5 steps left, and with only 1 step left for each sample. Moreover, the full-trajectory3 version of POJ-104/0/50 serves as the baseline training set. The detailed results are presented in the Table2. We observe that for all three GNN variants, training on datasets with only 5 or 10 steps achieves comparable generalization performance to training on the full-trajectory (50 steps) dataset. This favorable outcome can be attributed to the alignment between the iterative nature of the DFA algorithm and the iterative working pattern of GNNs. Each GNN layer only needs to mimic one iteration of the algorithm, allowing the entire GNN model, with its multiple layers, to naturally replicate the complete iterative process. As a result, a GNN does not have to learn from the repetitive complete execution trajectories — like human students, a few demonstration steps are suficient for efective learning. A notable distinction between DFA-GNN+, DFA-GNN, and DFA-GNN− emerges in the most extreme case, where only one step remains in each training sample. DFA-GNN+, the most aligned GNN, performs nearly flawlessly, while both DFA-GNN and DFA-GNN− fail completely on larger test samples, achieving a 0.00 last-step F1 score. If the GNNs are likened to human students, diferent variants with diferent levels of algorithmic alignment with the target DFA algorithm are like students with diferent levels of aptitude. DFA-GNN+ is like an exceptionally gifted student who, after learning just one step, excels on much more complex test cases. In contrast, DFA-GNN and DFA-GNN− are less adept at reasoning through the DFA algorithm, needing more than one step of training demonstration to reach their peak performance. Table 2. sections.title: 5.3 Experiment III: How about the sample eficiency of DFA-GNN<sup>+</sup>, DFA-GNN, and DFA-GNN<sup>−</sup>?
sections.text:
In the previous experiment, training on truncated, shorter trajectories and successfully generalizing to longer ones highlighted the advantage of using GNNs for the DFA reasoning task, especially those with high algorithmic alignment. This experiment further explores the sample eficiency of each GNN variant. We randomly selected a small subset of samples from the training set (POJ-104/0/50). Each model was then trained on these reduced datasets4 for plenty of epochs, with the best-performing epoch on the validation set subsequently tested on the representative POJ-104/500/600 test set. This process was repeated three times for each set size to calculate the mean and standard deviation, allowing for the inclusion of error bars. Fig. 5 shows the last-step F1 scores of DFA-GNN+, DFA-GNN, and DFA-GNN− on the vertical axis, plotted against the sizes of the simplified training sets (1, 10, 100, and 1,000 samples) on the horizontal axis. The performance of each model trained on the entire training set is also reported as a baseline. ![](images/f499d3152c6be81b23807c1279b02dcd7763daf30e555cd60662fb2a2acad9f7.jpg) Fig. 5. The last-step F1 score against the sizes of the training sets. The “full” indicates that the models are trained with the full POJ-104/0/50 training set. Fig. 5 illustrates that, when trained on the same dataset size, higher algorithmic alignment with the target DFA algorithm leads to better generalization performance. As the number of training samples increases, the performance of the GNN models tends to improve and stabilize. Notably, DFA-GNN+ and DFA-GNN achieve stable, comparable performance with only 100 samples, matching the performance of their counterpart trained on the full dataset. This indicates that these two GNN variants are highly sample-eficient for the DFA reasoning task. Conversely, DFA-GNN−, with the lowest algorithmic alignment to the DFA algorithm, requires significantly more training samples to reach competitive performance with its fully trained counterparts. sections.title: 5.5 Experiment V: How about comparing GNNs with LLMs?
sections.text:
Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) [41, 42, 43] have showcased their excep- tional capabilities on code-related tasks [44], such as code completion [45, 46], code repair [47, 48], and code synthesis [49]. Motivated by these successes, our final experiment seeks to investigate what if our GNN-based approaches are compared with LLMs on the DFA reasoning tasks. For this purpose, we select three cutting-edge LLMs: GPT-4o [41], DeepSeek-v3 [42], and Llama 3.3 [43], and evaluate their reasoning ability on the representative test dataset (POJ-104/500/600). Each specific DFA task (i.e., liveness analysis, dominance analysis, and control reachability analysis) and test sample are encoded into carefully designed natural language prompts to ensure compatibility with the LLMs. One notable observation from the LLM responses caught our attention: it is hard for them to return the complete information. LLMs appear to exhibit “impatient” behaviors, often omitting substantial portions of essential content, including the required results. For instance, a typical LLM response for a DFA task contains data-flow states of less than 20 nodes, whereas states of more than 500 nodes are required for each sample in POJ-104/500/600 — the omitted information tend to be replaced by placeholders such as ellipses (“...”) or phrases like “and so on”. To quantify the extent of this omission, we introduce the concept of the response ratio (abbreviated as RR), which is defined as the ratio between the number of data-flow states provided in the response and the total number of expected data-flow states. From the results presented in the Table 4, it is evident that GNN-based approaches outperform the LLMs. First, the response ratios of all three tested LLMs are pretty low. One contributing reason is that LLMs often adopt a human-like communication habit: omitting repetitive reasoning steps under the assumption that the listener can infer the omitted content. Another reason is the token limit imposed in each LLM request, which becomes particularly problematic for larger testing samples, where responses are truncated once they exceed the maximum token limit. In contrast, these issues are nonexistent for GNN-based approaches, which are specifically designed to process graph structures and are guaranteed to return all the states associated with each graph node (therefore, the response ratios of all GNN-based approaches are 100%). Second, the response correctness of the LLMs is far worse than that of GNN-based approaches, even significantly under-performing the least aligned model, DFA-GNN−. This discrepancy arises because the DFA reasoning process relies on complex graph reasoning, which remains a substantial challenge for current LLMs [50]. In conclusion, our GNN-based models perform much beter and are more consistent in handling DFA reasoning tasks than cuting-edge LLMs.

abstract: Recent advances in applying deep neural networks to programming tasks have achieved remarkable success in practice, prompting interest in exploring how well these models can perform traditional program analysis techniques. Data-flow analysis (DFA), a classic and well-established approach for analyzing programs, presents an opportunity to assess the capabilities of neural networks in this domain. Given the structural similarities between DFA and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), we explore the extent to which GNNs can effectively model the DFA algorithm. Building on the concept of algorithmic alignment from Neural Algorithmic Reasoning (NAR), we identify two key challenges: the noninterference property of the bit-vectors used in DFA and the complex handling of external information at different stages of the algorithm. Addressing these gaps, we propose three GNN architectures — DFA-GNN−, DFA-GNN, and DFA-GNN+ — that progressively align with the DFA algorithm. Our evaluations emphasize the generalization capacity of these models, particularly in scenarios where training occurs on smaller samples while testing on much larger inputs. Results demonstrate that GNNs with higher algorithmic alignment, such as DFA-GNN+, exhibit superior generalization and sample efficiency, accurately scaling to 10 times larger inputs with minimal training data. Notably, we show that GNNs trained with only input-output pairs can perform competitively with models trained using full execution trajectory supervision, a common practice in recent NAR studies. This finding highlights the efficiency and robustness of GNNs in reasoning tasks when algorithmically aligned with the target algorithm.

Before delving into the results, we will first outline the datasets and initial setup. Datasets preprocessing. The datasets used in this paper are derived from existing work PRO-GRAML [27], which provides control-flow graphs of program samples from multiple projects, such as POJ-104[39], TensorFlow [40], GitHub, and Linux. Before feeding these samples to GNNs, preprocessing is required. We choose a selection of specific DFA tasks that cover forward and backward, may and must tasks — liveness analysis, control reachability analysis, and dominance analysis. During preprocessing, three DFA tasks are applied sequentially to the program samples, generating the required auxiliary attributes, full execution trajectories, and final algorithm outputs. The produced execution trajectories are diverse in length and, thus should be further truncated or padded according to the demanding length ofeach experiment. When padding is needed, the padded content repeats the last states of the original trajectory, as these states represent the fixed-point, which remains unchanged even if execution continues [6]. This allows the padded trajectory to remain valid for training or testing, eliminating the need to track the original trajectory length for each sample. Dataset division. This paper focuses on the GNNs’ generalization ability in the DFA reasoning task. In all the experiments, the models are trained on relatively small samples but tested on larger input sizes. To facilitate this, we subdivide the original datasets based on the size of the samples (measured by statement count). Each dataset name used in this paper is composed of three parts, separated by slashes: the project name (e.g., POJ-104, GitHub, Linux, TensorFlow), followed by the range of statement counts in the samples. For instance, the training set POJ-104/0/50 includes all program samples from the POJ-104 project less than 50 statements, while the testing set POJ-104/500/600 contains samples with 500 to 600 statements, meaning the test samples are roughly ten times larger than those in the training set POJ-104/0/50. All datasets used, and their specific purposes, are detailed in the Appendix B. Please also note that the maximum trajectory lengths for each dataset before padding or truncation are provided in the table in Appendix B, along with the fixed trajectory length of each dataset after adjustment. For all test datasets, samples are padded to exceed the maximum trajectory length. However, this is not the case for the training datasets, as most experiments (Experiments 5.2, 5.3, and 5.4) require truncated trajectories for training. Training on shorter trajectories and testing on longer than complete ones, from this point of view can be seen as an exploration of the models generalization ability. Measurements. In our experiments, we evaluate GNNs not only by their performance on final outputs but also by how they perform at intermediate steps — a GNN can only be said to have “learned” the DFA algorithm if it produces the same intermediate data-flow states as the ground- truth execution trajectory. Therefore, except for the last-step precision (L-P), last-step recall (L-R), and last-step F1 score (L-F1), we also report the mean F1 score over all steps (M-F1) to measure the model’s faithfulness to the target algorithm. Notice. All the experiment results reported in this work are the average values over three realworld DFA tasks for compiler optimization: liveness analysis, control reachability analysis, and dominance analysis [1]. Detailed explanations for each task can be found in Appendix A. Please also note that the DFA algorithm itself, as a theoretically provable algorithm, is considered 100% correct. Consequently, the DFA-algorithm-generated results are implicitly employed as the groundtruth in all of our experiments. 5.1 Experiment I: With or without Trajectory supervision? In recent NAR research, there has been a trend of supervising models with additional ground-truth trajectories, which has led to noticeable improvements in reasoning ability [23, 25]. A plausible explanation is that these additional supervisions implicitly break down the original complex problem into smaller, more manageable sub-problems [17, 26]. When only input-output pairs are provided, the model must independently discover how to mimic the reasoning process, which is intuitively more challenging than training with trajectory supervision. Our first experiment investigates the two distinctive training modes: a) with trajectory supervision, and b) without trajectory supervision. Specifically, DFA-GNN+, DFA-GNN, and DFA-GNN− are respectively trained on POJ-104/0/50. Reflecting on how we learned DFA algorithms in class: the teacher would show students a few steps of calculating the next data-flow states based on the current ones, typically using simplified code examples with relatively few statements as demonstrations. After seeing a few examples, most students could handle the entire process, even when dealing with real-world samples containing hundreds of statements that require many steps to reach the final result. The clear advantages of human learners are their high sample eficiency and strong generalization ability across diferent sample sizes and execution trace lengths. Inspired by this, the experiment explores how DFA-GNN+, DFA-GNN, and DFA-GNN− perform when trained on smaller-scale samples with truncated, short trajectories, mimicking how human students learn. Specifically, we extract short continuous portions of trajectories from each sample in POJ-104/0/50, creating three new training datasets: POJ-104/0/50 with 10 steps left, with 5 steps left, and with only 1 step left for each sample. Moreover, the full-trajectory3 version of POJ-104/0/50 serves as the baseline training set. The detailed results are presented in the Table2. We observe that for all three GNN variants, training on datasets with only 5 or 10 steps achieves comparable generalization performance to training on the full-trajectory (50 steps) dataset. This favorable outcome can be attributed to the alignment between the iterative nature of the DFA algorithm and the iterative working pattern of GNNs. Each GNN layer only needs to mimic one iteration of the algorithm, allowing the entire GNN model, with its multiple layers, to naturally replicate the complete iterative process. As a result, a GNN does not have to learn from the repetitive complete execution trajectories — like human students, a few demonstration steps are suficient for efective learning. A notable distinction between DFA-GNN+, DFA-GNN, and DFA-GNN− emerges in the most extreme case, where only one step remains in each training sample. DFA-GNN+, the most aligned GNN, performs nearly flawlessly, while both DFA-GNN and DFA-GNN− fail completely on larger test samples, achieving a 0.00 last-step F1 score. If the GNNs are likened to human students, diferent variants with diferent levels of algorithmic alignment with the target DFA algorithm are like students with diferent levels of aptitude. DFA-GNN+ is like an exceptionally gifted student who, after learning just one step, excels on much more complex test cases. 5.4 Experiment IV: Can GNNs generalize across projects? All the evaluations so far have been limited to the POJ-104[39] project. In real-world scenarios, however, the DFA algorithm must work across diferent projects, which is a fundamental requirement for algorithmic robustness. Motivated by this, the experiment examines the cross-project generalization ability of DFA-GNN+, DFA-GNN, and DFA-GNN− to determine how GNNs with varying levels of algorithmic alignment to the DFA algorithm perform on new, unseen projects. Specifically, in addition to the project POJ-104[39], the GNNs are respectively trained on three other projects: GitHub, Linux, and TensorFlow [40]; and the trained models are further tested on each project. Training samples were selected from smaller-scale datasets (less than 50 statements each, i.e., POJ-104/0/50, GitHub/0/50, Linux/0/50, and TensorFlow/0/50), while testing samples were from larger-scale datasets (POJ-104/500/600, GitHub/500/600, Linux/500/600, and TensorFlow/500/600). The results are presented in Table 3, where underlined terms highlight the models’ performances when trained and tested on the same project, serving as baselines for comparisons with models trained and tested on diferent projects. Key observations include: 1) DFA-GNN+ demonstrates nearly perfect cross-project generalization, maintaining stable performance across all test sets regardless of the project it was trained on. 2) DFA-GNN also generalizes well across projects, though with slightly less stability than DFA-GNN+. On all the test sets, the DFA-GNNs get comparable, or even better performance when trained on diferent projects than when trained and tested on the same project. 3) DFA-GNN−, however, shows significant performance degradation in certain cases, especially when trained on POJ-104 but tested on GitHub, Linux, or TensorFlow. In summary, a GNN’s ability to generalize across projects is closely tied to its algorithmic alignment with the target DFA algorithm — higher alignment improves cross-project generalization. 5.5 Experiment V: How about comparing GNNs with LLMs? Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) [41, 42, 43] have showcased their excep- tional capabilities on code-related tasks [44], such as code completion [45, 46], code repair [47, 48], and code synthesis [49]. Motivated by these successes, our final experiment seeks to investigate what if our GNN-based approaches are compared with LLMs on the DFA reasoning tasks. For this purpose, we select three cutting-edge LLMs: GPT-4o [41], DeepSeek-v3 [42], and Llama 3.3 [43], and evaluate their reasoning ability on the representative test dataset (POJ-104/500/600). Each specific DFA task (i.e., liveness analysis, dominance analysis, and control reachability analysis) and test sample are encoded into carefully designed natural language prompts to ensure compatibility with the LLMs. One notable observation from the LLM responses caught our attention: it is hard for them to return the complete information. LLMs appear to exhibit “impatient” behaviors, often omitting substantial portions of essential content, including the required results. For instance, a typical LLM response for a DFA task contains data-flow states of less than 20 nodes, whereas states of more than 500 nodes are required for each sample in POJ-104/500/600 — the omitted information tend to be replaced by placeholders such as ellipses (“...”) or phrases like “and so on”. To quantify the extent of this omission, we introduce the concept of the response ratio (abbreviated as RR), which is defined as the ratio between the number of data-flow states provided in the response and the total number of expected data-flow states. From the results presented in the Table 4, it is evident that GNN-based approaches outperform the LLMs. First, the response ratios of all three tested LLMs are pretty low. One contributing reason is that LLMs often adopt a human-like communication habit: omitting repetitive reasoning steps under the assumption that the listener can infer the omitted content. Another reason is the token limit imposed in each LLM request, which becomes particularly problematic for larger testing samples, where responses are truncated once they exceed the maximum token limit. In contrast, these issues are nonexistent for GNN-based approaches, which are specifically designed to process graph structures and are guaranteed to return all the states associated with each graph node (therefore, the response ratios of all GNN-based approaches are 100%). Second, the response correctness of the LLMs is far worse than that of GNN-based approaches, even significantly under-performing the least aligned model, DFA-GNN−. This discrepancy arises because the DFA reasoning process relies on complex graph reasoning, which remains a substantial challenge for current LLMs [50]. In conclusion, our GNN-based models perform much beter and are more consistent in handling DFA reasoning tasks than cuting-edge LLMs.
